summary: Defines a method to authenticate Telnet using the Key Exchange Algorithm (KEA) and to encrypt the Telnet stream using SKIPJACK. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This describes a way for Telnet to prove identity and scramble text using two specific government-designed methods.

questions: how to use kea for telnet
subtitle: Secure Telnet authentication and encryption using government algorithms

tldr.problem: Telnet normally sends passwords in the clear and does not authenticate the server, making it vulnerable to eavesdropping and impersonation.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies how to use the Key Exchange Algorithm (KEA) for mutual authentication with X.509 certificates and the SKIPJACK cipher to encrypt the Telnet stream. Two modes are defined: one with stream integrity checking via SHA-1 hashing and one without.
tldr.outcome: Telnet connections can achieve mutual authentication and encrypted sessions, though this method was limited by export restrictions on SKIPJACK and is now obsolete in favor of SSH.

today: RFC 2951 is Informational and historical. SKIPJACK was restricted by export controls, and Telnet has been superseded by SSH for secure remote access.

sections.title: Telnet Security Limitations
sections.content:
Telnet, as originally defined, transmits data in the clear. It lacks any built-in concept of security and normally requires users to send their passwords unencrypted to the server. Worse, the server does not authenticate itself to the user, leaving room for impersonation attacks.

RFC 2941 defined the TELNET Authentication Option, which provides a framework for negotiating authentication methods and encryption between client and server. This RFC specifies a concrete implementation of that option using the Key Exchange Algorithm (KEA) and the SKIPJACK encryption algorithm to provide mutual authentication and session confidentiality.
sections.plainLanguage: Regular Telnet is like sending postcards: anyone can read them. This describes how to add a secret handshake and seal the messages in envelopes so only the right person can read them.

sections.title: Key Exchange and Certificates
sections.content:
The RFC specifies mutual authentication through the exchange of X.509 certificates containing KEA public keys. Each side sends its certificate first, and both sides validate the certificate before using the public key to establish a shared SKIPJACK encryption key.

The exchange also involves nonces (NonceA and NonceB), which are random 64-bit values chosen by each side, and initialization vectors (IVs), which are 24-byte random values used to initialize the SKIPJACK cipher. These random values prevent an attacker from replaying captured authentication exchanges.
sections.plainLanguage: Both the client and server prove who they are using special digital documents (certificates). They exchange random numbers to set up a secret key that only they know.

sections.title: SKIPJACK Encryption Modes
sections.content:
The RFC defines two distinct encryption modes for TELNET data after authentication succeeds. The first, KEA_SJ, uses SKIPJACK in Cipher Feedback mode on 8 bits (CFB-8), which provides confidentiality but no integrity checking. One byte of ciphertext is sent for each byte of plaintext.

The second mode, KEA_SJ_INTEG, uses CFB-32 with stream integrity. It computes a keyed hash (using SHA-1) of the data stream and appends the hash value to each character, requiring 4 bytes of ciphertext for every byte of plaintext. The receiving end verifies the hash to detect tampering or synchronization loss. If verification fails, the only safe recovery is to drop the connection and start over.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to scramble the data: fast but without error checking, or slower but with a checksum to catch if something got corrupted or tampered with.

sections.title: Authentication Exchange Sequence
sections.content:
The RFC describes a four-step exchange for each mode. In the initial step, the client sends its username and indicates which authentication type it chooses from the server's list. The client then sends its certificate and a public key component (Ra) to the server.

The server responds with its certificate, a public key component (Rb), an initialization vector (IVb), and an encrypted nonce. The client then sends an initialization vector (IVa) and an encrypted challenge. Finally, the server sends an encrypted response, and both sides begin encryption. The use of encryption as a side effect of successful authentication protects against active attackers who might otherwise hijack the session after authentication but before encryption begins.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server take turns sending messages to prove they are who they claim and to set up the secret key, step by step.

sections.title: Cryptographic Requirements and Risks
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that implementations must protect private keys and encryption keys from disclosure. It also warns that the quality of random number generation is critical: weak random number generators can make the keys easy to guess. The RFC references RFC 1750 and FIPS Pub 186 for guidance on generating cryptographic random numbers.

A key security decision is that encryption is linked to successful authentication: it cannot be negotiated separately. This prevents an attacker from exploiting a window of vulnerability between authentication completion and encryption negotiation. If encryption is disabled, the only safe way to restart it is to repeat the entire authentication process.
sections.plainLanguage: Random numbers must be truly random, not predictable. If an attacker can predict the random values, they can break the encryption. And once encryption starts, you cannot turn it off and back on safely—you have to start over completely.

sections.title: Historical Status
sections.content:
This RFC was published in September 2000 as Informational. It describes cryptographic algorithms (KEA and SKIPJACK) that were developed by the NSA for government use. Export restrictions on SKIPJACK and the complexity of implementing KEA made this method rarely deployed outside government and military contexts.

Telnet itself is now considered insecure and has been superseded by SSH, which combines authentication, encryption, and data integrity in a simpler, more standardized way. This RFC is primarily of historical interest and is not recommended for new implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: This method was too complicated and used algorithms that were restricted by law, so it was never widely used. SSH, a simpler system, became the standard way to securely log into computers instead.
